items.title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
items.abstract: An environmental health expert whose University of Iowa team will be testing the air downwind of the detonation site explains the risks people, pets and farms face.
paras: The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice . According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide , an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “ unacceptable risk of accidental detonation .” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as it blows for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed by the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026 . A federal appeals court paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations on Nov. 20 after two groups sued, but the Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan. We asked him about the risks and what happens to the lead in an explosion.
What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets .

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children . If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies , including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth , where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body . That’s a pretty strong statement.
What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23 , the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
What can people do to stay safe in those areas?
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.
What is your team planning for testing?

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.

This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-funded centers have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.
Patrick O'Shaughnessy receives funding from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences

items.title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
items.abstract: The post Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology? appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise , particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage . CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.
At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.
Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?
Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:
Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.

I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.
So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:

Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.

In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.

Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”

Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”

When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal.

In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions, but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it happen.

One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook, not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.

A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.
“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an alien,” Riahi said.

The 2008 and 2010 projections are from the IEA’s Blue Map scenario; a second 2010 projection is from the Net Zero by 2050 scenario; 2018 is from the Sustainable Development scenario; and 2021 , 2022 , 2023 and 2024 are from the Announced Pledges, Stated Policies and Net Zero by 2050 scenarios. Some of these scenarios represent pathways designed to achieve a specific temperature or concentration of CO2. Other scenarios represent what is possible based on current policies or pledges. Pathways from years where underlying data was not provided in the IEA’s report were excluded.
The post Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology? appeared first on ProPublica .

paras: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole , wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat , a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation , an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation , established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha , a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook , authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh , the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end . As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people , and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya , a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country , and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters ; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.

items.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
items.abstract: About 1 in 4 US adults are family caregivers.
paras: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.
“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
A growing trend
One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.
My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .
Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”
Family caregivers pay a price

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.
A ‘daughterhood penalty’

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

items.title: The ongoing efforts to get ecocide recognized at the International Criminal Court
items.abstract: For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them.
paras: Activists want to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment and punish those responsible for defiling it
Originally published on Global Voices

An aerial view of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the largest marine oil spill in history. Under the proposed ICC amendment, oil company executives could be held accountable in such cases. Image via Wikimedia Commons . CC BY-SA 2.0 .

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law ( HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation , ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “ digital nation ” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu , says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations .
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations. Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook . Fair use.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S. , China , and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.
Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019. In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said :

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”
A protest poster against ecocide shaming oil giants at a climate protest in Maryland in 2017. Photo from Wikimedia Commons . CC BY-SA 2.0 .

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals , such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.
As an editorial in The Global Witness notes:

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement . It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself .

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue , the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) at The Hague. Photo via Wikimedia Commons . CC BY 2.0 .
Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

In December 2025, ICC prosecutors published a policy paper on prosecuting environmental damage through the pre-existing mechanisms already laid out in the Rome Statute — the international treaty which established the ICC.

The Rome Statute mentions the environment exactly one time. Article 8(2)(b)(iv) makes it a war crime to launch an attack knowing it will cause “ widespread, long-term and severe ” damage to the environment. Traditionally, this article has applied only during armed conflict, and previous attempts to prosecute environmental destruction at the court have been unsuccessful.
Vanuatu’s ambassador to the UN, Odo Tevi, has argued that the reckless destruction of nature “can and does take place at any time, not just during conflict.”

The December 2025 policy, launched at the Assembly of States Parties, was co-hosted by Costa Rica, France, Germany, Panama, and the Marshall Islands. It explains how environmental destruction can be investigated and prosecuted within the four existing crime categories, for example, when pollution or the seizure of natural resources is used to commit a crime against humanity.

Analysts at the Conflict and Environment Observatory note that this policy paper does not address the ecocide proposal and that ambiguity in the war crime standard remains. Others point to limited resources at the prosecutor’s office.

In September 2026, ICC representatives said they had “ moved into the implementation stage ” to establish clearer parameters for prosecuting environmental crimes under the Rome Statute. In its statement, the office said it had received numerous communications about alleged crimes with an environmental dimension and was building a network of environmental law enforcement authorities, relevant organizations, expert groups, and civil society organizations to investigate.

But some jurisdictions are not waiting. As one recent study notes , “the substance of ecocide criminalization has advanced everywhere except through the amendment: an EU directive whose gravest offense is officially ‘comparable to “ecocide,”’ a Council of Europe convention, national codes in Belgium, France and Ukraine, and a completed OTP [ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor] policy that prosecutes environmental damage through the existing four crimes.”

Counts vary depending on how many states currently employ domestic laws against ecocide. Stop Ecocide International says twelve countries, including Belgium , France, and Ukraine, have adopted ecocide or equivalent offenses into domestic law. Mauritius became the most recent in April 2026, and legislation is progressing in countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, Italy, and the Netherlands. As noted in the aforementioned study, the EU’s revised Environmental Crime Directive also covers conduct “ comparable to ecocide ,” and member states had to transpose it by May 2026.

The next stage is procedural rather than dramatic: Whether states give the proposal a formal path forward at the Assembly of States Parties’ 25th session in The Hague, from November 30 to December 7, 2026. A vote would signal whether the Rome Statute can grow beyond the atrocities it was written for. A stall would leave the prosecutor’s policy and national laws as the main tools available.
The decision comes at a crucial time for the ICC, as some international stakeholders begin to question the legitimacy, power, and effectiveness of international ruling bodies.

For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them. Until that infrastructure is implemented, the burden of harm will continue to fall on those least responsible for causing this crisis.

items.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
items.abstract: Medicare and Medicaid provide limited help with caregiving for older adults – and that means unpaid relatives often bear big burdens.
paras: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?
The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.
While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.
Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements .

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.
Medicaid can help, but access is limited
Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.
However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services .
Who provides care in the meantime?
There’s a shortage of paid caregivers

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born .
The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.
Caregiving often has financial consequences
When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.
Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.
Families often have to shoulder responsibility

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage .

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

items.title: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
items.abstract: After slashing foreign aid for the promotion of democracy, the State Department is giving $1 million to AfriForum, an NGO that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.
paras: The U.S. State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.

The grant, first reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026 , would support research to document the “ hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” experienced by Afrikaners – descendants of white Dutch settlers who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.
As scholars who study foreign aid and civil society organizations , we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs the U.S. has funded in the past .
Supporting democracy by funding NGOs
The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and strengthen human rights protections .

Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy.

Past administrations called this assistance “ fundamental ” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost $3 billion annually .

Some of this money has supported NGOs engaged in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where civil society is especially at risk .
NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help stave off future violence .
Slashing foreign aid
The Trump administration suspended most U.S. foreign aid in January 2025 , soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.

It then dismantled USAID , the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending . It has continued to take steps in that direction with or without lawmakers’ cooperation .
As a result, many lifesaving public health programs lost funding. This policy change has had an enormous human toll , which public health researchers have begun to quantify .

In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. USAID’s Democracy Fund , which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s funding and staffing for promoting democracy were also slashed .
Claiming there’s a ‘white genocide’

In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the benefits of these efforts . The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.
By contrast, AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history , without any evident effort to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa.
It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “ white genocide ” in that country.

In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be victims of crime and other forms of violence compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa.
By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the dubious claims the group makes about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.

And the Trump administration’s embrace of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U.S. has allowed thousands of white South Africans to come to the U.S. as refugees while denying admission to nearly all other refugees from the rest of the world.

items.title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
items.abstract: Philosopher Søren Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on faith and existentialism, but love is also a central focus.
paras: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor , I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher , I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two .

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism , which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.
Aesthetic love

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “ aesthetic ” and “ ethical ” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote .

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires , not principles.
Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction : a pattern that we feel compelled to continue , despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction ,” and whether love can become one , but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two .

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.
At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “ a kind of despair ,” rooted in estrangement from oneself , a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.
Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.
Ethical love

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “ Either/Or ” and in “ Works of Love ,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.
Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love .”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote .

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves , a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.

items.title: El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn
items.abstract: What happens on the slopes in Chile holds clues for the western US snow season. But all that precipitation can also bring trouble.
paras: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, bringing lots of snow to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season . But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

I’m an avid skier and snow scientist at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be one of the strongest El Niños on record , let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.
The pros and cons of all that precipitation
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns around the world.

It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was 2.5 C warmer (36.5 F , making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.

In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.
That pattern is almost exactly what’s being forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27 . It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.

Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread destructive flooding in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. Fast-melting snow and days of heavy rain flooded the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.
Recovering from last year’s snow drought
Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered one of the lowest snow years on record for almost the entire western United States.

Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled . The two biggest – Lake Powell and Lake Mead – together supply water for about 40 million people and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.

The very low snowfall, as well as unusually warm midwinter temperatures that drove sublimation – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by record-high summer temperatures .
Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to alleviate a long-running drought that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.

In a positive sign, Lake Powell rose with the recent rains. Overall, the Super El Niño conditions being forecast for 2026-27 are expected to bring more than average rain and snow this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.
What happens in Chile …
Snow scientists like me keep an eye on the South American winter in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.
Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.

South America saw a huge amount of snow , particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some areas like Portillo , the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.

The snow was a boon for Chile’s ski resorts . Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and extended its ski season , originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an explosion of spring flowers .

Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to pick up more moisture in this zone than usual , and this brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest .

If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.

items.title: Preventable vision loss affects more than a billion people globally - and uneven access to care is the major culprit
items.abstract: As the global population ages, the number of people suffering from vision loss is expected to increase.
paras: Around the world, more than 1 billion people are living with vision loss in their daily lives. For many, this means they don’t have the glasses they need to see clearly. For others, conditions such as cataracts , glaucoma , macular degeneration or diabetic eye disease have caused vision loss.
The burden of this problem is not shared equally – 55% of those experiencing vision loss are women and girls, 73% are ages 50 and older , and 90% live in low- and middle-income countries .

Age is the most important risk factor for vision loss . Since global populations are rapidly aging , the number of people experiencing vision loss is expected to increase to more than 1.7 billion by 2050.
So this public health threat is growing. Yet, it’s also almost entirely avoidable.

We are both population health researchers , and one of us is an opthamologist . We also lead the Michigan Sensory Health and Aging Research Collaborative at the University of Michigan, where we have spent years working to advance vision and eye health for underserved populations in the U.S. and globally. Recent developments give us hope that real progress is within reach.
A smart investment

Losing vision quite literally affects how people see the world, and it also increases their risk of other health issues , including falls, depression and even dementia. The risk of mortality is more than twice as high for adults living with vision loss.

The upside is that about 80% of vision loss can be reversed or prevented with timely detection and treatment. In fact, most cases can be fixed with eyeglasses or cataract surgery, two of the most cost-effective interventions in all of healthcare.

A recent report showed that eye care is not only important for health and well-being, but it is also a smart investment: Every dollar that low- and middle-income countries invest in eye health returns US$28 to their economies . This makes eye health easily one of the best deals in global health and development.
A development problem with a financial upside

Back in 1999, the World Health Organization launched an initiative called VISION 2020: The Right to Sight . The aim was to draw attention and resources to vision and eye health problems, including those that would affect an aging global population.

More recently, in 2021, 193 United Nations member countries unanimously ratified a resolution calling on governments and international financial institutions to improve access to eye care and to provide the resources to make this possible.

In addition, this resolution acknowledged the central role of vision and eye health in achieving the U.N. sustainable development goals , a set of 17 ambitious aims, including universal access to food, clean water, education and work. Reframing vision and eye health as a development issue with a massive financial upside put the problem in front of people from a variety of sectors, such as education, labor and economics, and encouraged them to imagine how they could be a part of the solution.

In the five years since that resolution passed, the eye health sector has evolved some innovative strategies. For example, the new Vision Catalyst Fund brings together large-scale donors, nongovernmental organizations and local medical providers to test new approaches to paying for eye care and getting it to those most in need.

Another organization that has emerged to tackle avoidable vision loss is Peek Vision , a U.K.-based charity that began as a simple smartphone app. This app can be used by anyone with access to a smartphone to screen vision. So far, it has been used to screen more than 18 million people for vision loss and has connected more than 1.5 million to eye care. The organization is hoping to screen a million people per week by 2029.
Building momentum

In November 2026, the government of Antigua and Barbuda hosted the first-ever Global Summit for Eye Health , in collaboration with the governments of Nigeria, Guyana, Ireland and Bangladesh and the WHO. Policymakers, nongovernmental organizations, heads of state and global organizations such as the U.N., WHO and World Bank attended, with an eye toward a singular goal – ending avoidable sight loss worldwide.

The summit’s goal was to bring together key players from across the eye health sector. Governments and organizations are being asked to make forward-looking commitments toward accelerating progress. For example, 48 governments committed to embedding eye health in their national health systems, while health ministries, NGOs and eye hospitals have committed to providing cataract surgery and eyeglasses to tens of millions of people over the next few years.

The evidence to drive this investment is already there: Trials have shown that vision care for kids boosts educational outcomes . In middle-aged and older adults, research shows that an inexpensive pair of reading glasses boosts productivity and economic earnings in the agricultural , garment and artisan industries.
Affording eye care in the US

While low- and middle-income countries contend with the overwhelming majority of vision loss, the problem is also significant in the U.S., where an estimated 32.2 million people contend with vision loss .

Older adults are by far the most affected group. While they benefit from Medicare coverage for medical issues such as cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration, major gaps remain, including unequal access to advanced eye care and inconsistent coverage of eyeglasses by Medicare.

Under traditional Medicare, eyeglasses are covered only once in a beneficiary’s lifetime, following cataract surgery. Otherwise, glasses can be a large – and recurring – out-of-pocket expense. With a pair of glasses costing an average of US$200-$370 in the U.S., compared with roughly $35 in China or India , clear eyesight may be financially out of reach for many older Americans. Low-cost online retailers have helped to disrupt this market, but accessing glasses through those websites still requires internet access and a credit or debit card.

Older adults dealing with common issues such as cataracts or refractive error , which causes blurry vision, are at higher risk for all sorts of costly downstream health issues, including falls and dementia . Each year in the U.S., 2.3 million older adults wind up in the ER for a fall, and nearly 1 million are admitted to the hospital, costing the healthcare system about $20 billion . When it comes to dementia, the costs are even greater , at around $750 billion dollars per year.

Financing more comprehensive eye care for older Americans is actually in everyone’s best interest. In fact, every dollar that public programs such as Medicare invest in treating refractive error and cataracts in older Americans is likely to return $9 to the U.S. economy. Annually, this equates to around $23 billion. This return on investment comes in the form of increased economic productivity, medical cost savings, fewer falls and fewer people with dementia.

Being able to see clearly is essential to overall health and well-being. The data is clear, that regardless of a country’s level of wealth, it makes sense to put resources toward vision and eye health.

items.title: Paid sick leave laws are no guarantee for Philly’s immigrant restaurant workers
items.abstract: Doctor’s note requirements, industry norms and fear of retaliation prevent many immigrant restaurant workers in Philadelphia from using paid sick leave.
paras: What do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day .

There is no federal right to paid sick leave . However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide , requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees.
In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck.
For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy.

I study restaurant work , an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born . Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala.

I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez .

Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015 . During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act , a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees.

A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees.
What I found , though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers.
‘$300 for a simple flu’

Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “ reasonable documentation ” – but only after an absence of more than two days.
Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance.

If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them.

Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.”

What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said.
Different policies for back-of-house workers

In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America.

The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid.

In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white.
I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers.

“The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.”
In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born.
Fear of retaliation

Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about.

Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves.

“The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’”
Healthy workers, healthy public

My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California .

Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. Paid sick leave makes for healthier workers , and healthier workers make for a healthier public .

items.title: How a Pittsburgh-born umpire painted baseball history onto the ball itself
items.abstract: A Pittsburgh-born umpire turned folk artist spent decades inking players, stats and legendary moments onto baseballs, turning them into miniature monuments.
paras: Baseballs are charismatic objects. It is no accident that the narrative spine of novelist Don DeLillo’s magnum opus of 20th-century American life , “Underworld,” involves the ownership of the baseball from the “shot heard ’round the world” – the ninth-inning home run New York Giants slugger Bobby Thomson hit to beat the Brooklyn Dodgers for the 1951 National League pennant. A lot of Americana has been projected onto the surface of a baseball.

But the surface of a baseball is not typically a canvas. The 26 or so square inches of area, created when two pieces of leather are connected with 108 red stitches , are awkward surfaces on which to draw. And most of the time, the only thing people want drawn on baseballs is a signature from an admired player.
But that’s not how George Sosnak saw them.

Born in Pittsburgh in 1924, Sosnak worked as a minor league umpire starting in his 30s, but he became better known as a self-taught artist over the subsequent four decades. Each baseball offered Sosnak at least four spaces to fill with images of players, team insignia or text recounting playing statistics or triumphs, all meticulously rendered in India ink.
An ongoing exhibit at the Westmoreland Museum of American Art features over 60 of the approximately 800 balls he finished painting in his lifetime – he began painting nearly 3,000 balls.

Sosnak’s creations are often colorful, depicting players in action, with facts about them or their games written alongside. Many of the baseballs function as miniature stories, a spherical, secular altarpiece that tells the story of a key game or season.
His “ Pittsburgh Pirates, 1978 ” ball features Harold “Pie” Traynor , Bill Mazeroski and Roberto Clemente .

Traynor and Clemente had both died in 1972, the year Mazeroski retired, and the three never played on a single team together. Depicting three of Sosnak’s most legendary hometown Pirates together created a kind of pantheon, with the timeless image of Clemente finishing his swing juxtaposed with the specific moment Mazeroski raised his hat while circling the bases after hitting the home run that won the 1960 World Series .

Sosnak’s scenes often involve these juxtapositions, using the raised seams and the uneven leather strips to both separate and connect moments for artistic effect. He even depicted something other than baseball itself on the balls, including other sports. But his main focus was on using the spherical leather canvas to memorialize the moments and people that mattered to Sosnak – and to fellow fans who commissioned the balls. He often used such detail – spectators in Forbes Field represented by tiny ink dashes – that magnifying glasses are required to fully appreciate the nuances.

Sosnak linked the American folk art tradition with the talismanic nature of an actual baseball. Unlike the case in most other professional sports, some fans come away from baseball games with balls as souvenirs — whether they were hit as home runs or foul balls, or just tossed into the crowd by players.

Baseballs are disposable – most balls last only a few pitches, so around 100 balls are used in every professional game – and yet they become treasured relics when caught. Sosnak’s painted balls combine these tensions: You can hold one in your hand, visualizing its past while touching the otherwise disposable object that was imparted meaning only through the triumph.
